Exhibitor | Museo Del Novecento, MilannnAbstract Art New WavesnnThe 1950s and early 1960s were marked by an economic boom, as illustrated in Arnaldo Pomodoro's La colonna del viaggiatore (The Traveller's Column), a dynamic cog intended to convey the future-oriented drive of early space explorations and the underlying anxiety associated with change. Artists experimented more and more and seemingly favoured abstract research, taking the resources of their languages to extremes. Sculptor Consagra chose a frontal sculpture, like a painting, while painters Accardi or Capogrossi work on varied repetitions of the same element, with the effect of captivating viewers' perception. Accardi's patterns appear as a chained generation of signs, conceived as the life-like equivalent of micro-organisms and cosmic bodies becoming and clustering. What counts for Capogrossi instead is the size variation of the signs in the pattern in order to create a sense of movement and depth of space, even in the flatness of the canvas. On another front, work focuses on enhancing the specific inherent expressiveness of materials used. Such a choice mostly results in a focus on existential confession, with the artwork becoming a record of one's physical, imaginative and emotional presence.nnThe paintings by Turcato, Scialoja, Novelli, attentive to the techniques of Neo-Dada collage, look at canvases as palimpsests, used to impress material-gestural traces, in a spatialization of the inner time of one's own, indefinite memories. The challenge for Scarpitta and Uncini is whether to produce more paintings and how to make them: by weaving strips of canvas to replace dynamic linear paths, or by working on concrete panels, as tactile versions of monochrome painting. Kounellis deals with figurative painting as an iconoclast: his Rosa (Rose) is not the one seen in real life yet a mere simplified sign of a concept.
